pairs.subject: prompt-assembly
pairs.evidence: src/lib/mcp/tools.ts:534 The scope-model copy on every tools/list result is hand-written prose that lists which tools each scope unlocks, and it names only two of the three followups:write tools: get_fix_brief (scopes ["mcp:read", "followups:write"], tools.ts:271) is missing, and tools.test.ts:164-166 only checks for selected substrings, so nothing derives this list from MCP_TOOLS or checks that it is complete.

techniques.evidence: src/lib/mcp/tools.ts:534 The catalog itself is a single authority: bindings are pinned to MCP_TOOLS and admitTools renders only active tools. The doctrine enumeration in TOOLS_LIST_SCOPE_COPY is a second, hand-written copy, it leaves out get_fix_brief, and no sync or completeness check covers it.
src/lib/mcp/handlers.ts:358 The comment on the per-entry field names its consumer (cite_memory) right where the field is attached.
src/lib/mcp/registry-reads.ts:134 find_skills returns index entries (name, description, registryPath, registryVersion) and never the body. The body comes only through get_skill, on demand.

src/lib/mcp/tools.ts:77 Each tool declares the trust class of its result (org-authored or computed) in the catalog. The field is required, so the class is set where the tool is declared rather than at a call site, and org-authored results go through egress redaction.

src/lib/mcp/tools.ts:102 Only the determinism precondition applies here: catalog order is alphabetical and pinned by a test, so the tool block stays byte-identical. The server holds no session, so the session-gate part does not apply.

pairs.registryProposal: capability-documentation assumes the system that renders the capability layer also owns the assembler. An MCP server publishes the layer but not the prompt, and its catalog-level `_meta` prose is a place where doctrine mentions drift. The technique could name server-published catalog copy explicitly as a doctrine surface that needs the same sync and completeness check.
